title: Manoj Bajpayee Is Playing the Man Who Saved India From Bankruptcy. Governor Arrives June 12.
excerpt: Set during the 1991 economic crisis, Governor stars Bajpayee as RBI Governor S. Venkitaramanan — the civil servant who stared down national insolvency while politicians panicked. Amit Trivedi scored it. Javed Akhtar wrote the lyrics. Your parents lived through it.
body:
There was a time before malls. Before Coke. Before you could buy more than one brand of toothpaste. If you grew up in India in the 1980s, you know this. If you didn't — if you're a second-generation NRI who has only ever known the India of IT parks and iPhone launches — **Governor** is about to introduce you to the country your parents actually left.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=LH4bC6P0az4</youtube>

**Manoj Bajpayee** plays **S. Venkitaramanan**, the Reserve Bank of India Governor who, in 1991, found himself staring at an economy with barely two weeks of foreign exchange reserves left. India was days away from defaulting on its international obligations. The country your parents built careers in — the one that now has a GDP north of $4 trillion — was, in that moment, functionally broke.

Directed by **Chinmay Mandlekar** — the Marathi cinema powerhouse behind *Dhurala* and the cultural phenomenon *Zapatlela 2* — and produced by **Vipul Amrutlal Shah**, the film dramatises the institutional warfare that played out behind closed doors as India teetered on the edge.

## The Story India Almost Forgot

The crisis was real, and it was terrifying. Foreign exchange reserves had plummeted to roughly $1.2 billion — barely enough to cover two weeks of imports. The government was forced to pledge 67 tonnes of gold to the Bank of England and the Union Bank of Switzerland just to stay solvent. The political establishment was in disarray. Three prime ministers served in the span of two years.

At the centre of it all was a career bureaucrat who believed, with absolute conviction, that if he failed, India failed.

> "I was always a news junkie. I know for a fact that it happened. But I don't have any knowledge of what went on behind the closed doors, and who were the people responsible for getting India out of that crisis." — Manoj Bajpayee

The film follows Venkitaramanan as he navigates political pressure, bureaucratic obstruction, and institutional resistance to avert sovereign default. **Adah Sharma** plays journalist Aditi Verma, and **Noushad Mohamed Kunju** appears as C. Rangarajan, who would eventually succeed Venkitaramanan as RBI Governor and oversee the liberalisation reforms.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZPaJjbuDYD/

## Bajpayee Googled His Way Into the Role

In a detail that is both disarming and entirely on-brand, Bajpayee admitted in a recent podcast that he had to look up basic economics terminology before every scene. "What does it mean that we have a deficit balance of 1.5 billion?" he said. "I didn't understand it. But as an actor, everything I deliver has to be believable."

This is the same man who disappeared into Bhiku Mhatre, into Sardar Khan, into a hundred roles where the preparation was invisible and the performance was shattering. That he approached macroeconomics with the same intensity he brings to underworld dons says something about the kind of actor he remains at 57.

Mandlekar's direction reportedly demanded painstaking period recreation. The production team worked to eliminate every trace of the modern world — no contemporary cars, no current signage, no anachronistic technology. "A lot of effort went to eliminate everything that looked like the modern world," the makers said.

## The Diaspora Angle Is Built In

Here is the thing about the 1991 crisis: it created the India that the diaspora lives alongside today. The liberalisation reforms that followed — championed by Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister — opened the economy, launched the IT revolution, and set in motion the chain of events that brought Indian professionals to Silicon Valley, to the NHS, to Bay Street.

Every NRI parent who worked at Infosys, TCS, or Wipro in the 1990s was a direct beneficiary of the crisis that this film depicts. Every H-1B visa holder in Sunnyvale or Edison exists, in some structural sense, because the events of 1991 forced India to change. **Governor** is the origin story of modern India's economic identity, and for diaspora audiences, it is the origin story of their own professional lives abroad.

Bajpayee has been making a direct appeal to younger viewers. In a video released this week, he addressed students: "Be the Governor of the future. India's future is safe in your hands." The message feels less like a marketing push and more like a civics lesson from a man who has never done anything cynically.

## The Music and the Moment

**Amit Trivedi** composed the score. **Javed Akhtar** wrote the lyrics. That pairing alone — the man who scored *Dev D* and *Queen* with the poet who wrote *Silsila* and *Lakshya* — signals ambition. This is not a film that treats its subject as a history textbook. It wants you to feel the walls closing in.

The film arrives on June 12 alongside **Main Vaapas Aaunga**, **Bharat Bhhagya Vidhaata**, and **Haunted 3D: Echoes of the Past**. It is the quietest of the four, the one without a superstar or a horror gimmick. It has Manoj Bajpayee, a true story, and the kind of premise that makes you text your parents afterwards.

That might be enough.

**Governor** releases in cinemas on June 12, 2026. Produced by Sunshine Pictures.
